---
title: "Data protection and security"
---

> **This page is a stub.** It sets out the rules that cover USRDS data, the
> ways data most often leaks during an analysis, and what usRds does about
> them today. It will grow as the package adds its own data-safety checks
> (see [issue #49](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/usRds/issues/49)).

## The rules

USRDS files are patient-level records released under a data use agreement
(DUA). Your DUA is the rule that applies. This page does not replace it, and
nothing in usRds makes an analysis compliant on its own. If this page and your
DUA disagree, follow your DUA.

Most DUAs set rules on three things:

- **Where the data may be stored.** Only on the systems the DUA approves.
- **Who may see it.** Only the people named on the DUA.
- **What may be shared.** Usually only aggregate results, with small cells
  suppressed. The
  [CMS Cell Size Suppression Policy](https://resdac.org/articles/cms-cell-size-suppression-policy),
  which applies to Medicare data, does not allow cells of 1 to 10 to be shown,
  or values from which such a cell could be worked out.

## The risks

Data rarely leaks through one dramatic mistake. It usually leaks through an
ordinary step in the work that makes a copy somewhere the DUA does not cover.

### Copies you did not count as data

Parquet files made by `convert_usrds_to_parquet()`, extracts saved as `.rds`,
`.csv` or `.parquet`, and cohort data frames are all USRDS data under your
DUA, just like the original SAS and CSV files. Keep every copy inside the
approved storage location.

### Folders that sync or back up

A folder on a network share, a mapped drive, or a folder synced by a service
such as OneDrive or Dropbox sends its files off your machine, whatever
program wrote them. Backup services do the same. Make sure every folder you
read from or write to, and any service that syncs or backs it up, is approved
for USRDS data.

### Data committed to a code repository

A data file committed to git is copied to every clone and to any remote such
as GitHub, and it stays in the repository's history even after you delete it.
Keep the USRDS folder outside any git repository. If data files do have to
sit inside a project folder, add ignore rules before the first commit, for
example:

```
# .gitignore: never commit data
*.sas7bdat
*.parquet
*.csv
*.rds
*.RData
*.rda
```

Adapt the list to your project: a rule such as `*.csv` also ignores public
CSV files you may want to commit. Check `git status` before each commit.

### The saved workspace and history

An `.RData` file saved when R closes can hold every patient-level data frame
from the session, and `.Rhistory` can hold values you printed. In RStudio,
set *Tools > Global Options > General > Save workspace to .RData on exit* to
**Never**, and turn off *Restore .RData into workspace at startup*.

### Paths in shared code

A data path written into a shared script can reveal where restricted data is
stored, and it breaks the script on anyone else's machine. Call
`set_USRDS_wd()` once (or with `permanent = TRUE`) instead.

### Small cells in results

Tables, figures and model output can identify people when counts are small,
even though they contain no identifiers. Check every output against the cell
size rule in your DUA before you share it.

### Web tools and AI assistants

Pasting rows, uploading files, or sharing screenshots of USRDS data with a
web service, including an AI coding assistant, sends the data to that
service. Do not do it unless your DUA allows it. Code, error messages with
values removed, and made-up example data are safer ways to get help.

## What usRds does today

- **It reads only the folder you name.** `set_USRDS_wd()` records the folder
  in the environment variable `USRDS_WD` and maps the files in it by name.
  When `USRDS_WD` is already set, loading the package maps the same folder
  again. Mapping reads file names only, not file contents.
- **It has no upload or telemetry feature.** usRds makes no network
  connections of its own.
- **It writes only where you tell it to.**
  - `convert_usrds_to_parquet()` writes Parquet files to the `target_dir` you
    give it, and nowhere else.
  - `set_USRDS_wd(permanent = TRUE)` adds one line to your `~/.Renviron` file:
    the folder path, not any data. With the default `permanent = FALSE`,
    nothing is written.
- **Results stay in your R session** until you save them. Data frames
  returned by the `get_*()` and cohort functions are patient-level.

What it does not do yet: usRds does not check whether your folders are
synced or shared, whether data sits inside a git repository, or whether a
result has small cells. Those checks are your responsibility for now.

## Planned protections

The plan in [issue #49](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/usRds/issues/49)
adds checks to the package itself. Names are provisional and none of these
exist yet:

- a read-only data-safety check when the package is attached, which notes
  missing protections in a git repository and warns (by path only) about
  data-like files that would be committed; turn it off with
  `options(usRds.safety_check = FALSE)`;
- the same check in `set_USRDS_wd()` and `convert_usrds_to_parquet()`;
- `check_repo_for_usrds_data()`, which scans a folder for files that look
  like USRDS data;
- opt-in helpers to add ignore rules and a pre-commit check to a project;
- `check_small_cells()`, which reports cells below a threshold (fewer than
  11 by default) in data frames, tables, plots and survival fits, without
  changing them.

This page will be updated as each one is added.
